Incorrect. 24.7 is not in the table; the 500 µmol row shows 25.4.
Incorrect. 30.1 is higher than every value in the table (the maximum is 26.1 at 750 µmol).

ox: Wrong. Hexokinase is the first step and traps glucose in the cell as G6P, but G6P can still go to glycogen or the pentose phosphate pathway. It is not the committed step.
Correct. PFK-1 turns fructose-6-phosphate into fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. After this step the sugar is committed to glycolysis. It is slowed by ATP and sped up by AMP and F2,6BP.
Wrong. Pyruvate kinase is regulated, but it is the last step, after the commitment has already been made.
Wrong. This enzyme starts the pentose phosphate pathway, a different route. Do not confuse it with glycolysis.

p: Glycolysis breaks glucose into pyruvate. The committed step is the one after which the molecule has no other option but to continue down the pathway. It is usually also the slowest, regulated step.
In glycolysis this is PFK-1. ATP signals the cell has enough energy and turns it down. AMP signals low energy and turns it up.

q14.eli: Think of a one-way toll gate on a highway. Once your car goes through, you cannot take any exit but the one ahead.
mem: PFK-1: F6P to F1,6BP is the committed, rate-limiting step.
ATP and citrate inhibit PFK-1; AMP and F2,6BP activate it.
Hexokinase = first step; pyruvate kinase = last step.
q14.trap: Choosing hexokinase because it is first. First is not the same as committed.

ox: Correct. Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but spends 2 early on, so the net is 2 ATP. It also makes 2 NADH.
Wrong. 4 ATP is the gross yield. You must subtract the 2 ATP invested in the first steps.
Wrong. About 30-32 ATP is the total from complete aerobic breakdown (glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, TCA cycle, electron transport chain).
Wrong. Glycolysis makes NADH. FADH2 is made in the TCA cycle and in fatty acid oxidation.

p: Glycolysis splits one glucose into two pyruvate. Early steps spend 2 ATP to prepare the sugar. Later steps make 4 ATP.
Net means what is left after paying the cost. It also makes 2 NADH, an electron carrier that can later be used to make more ATP.

q15.eli: You pay 2 dollars to enter a game and win 4 dollars. You walked away with 2 dollars of profit.
mem: Glycolysis net: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, 2 pyruvate.
Gross ATP = 4; invested = 2.
Aerobic total is about 30-32 ATP.

fm.f: Net ATP = ATP made - ATP spent
fm.why: Net yield means profit after the investment.

q15.trap: Reporting the gross 4 ATP instead of the net 2 ATP.

ox: Wrong. Complex I is blocked by rotenone, not cyanide.
Correct. Cyanide binds the iron in complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), so electrons cannot pass to O2. The whole chain backs up and O2 use stops.
Wrong. ATP synthase is blocked by oligomycin. That would stop ATP making but the chain problem is different.
Wrong. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) is inhibited by malonate, not cyanide.

p: The electron transport chain is a line of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons are passed down the line and finally given to oxygen at complex IV, forming water.
If complex IV is blocked, electrons cannot leave the chain. Everything upstream backs up and oxygen is no longer used.

q16.eli: It is like a bucket line passing water to the end person. If the last person is stuck, the whole line stops.
mem: Cyanide (and CO, azide) block complex IV.
Rotenone blocks complex I; malonate blocks complex II.
Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase.
q16.trap: Mixing up which poison blocks which complex. Oxygen is the final acceptor, so the O2-related poison hits complex IV.

ox: Correct. A proton leak is an uncoupler. The gradient cannot build, so the chain runs faster to try to fix it and uses more O2. ATP synthase has little gradient to use, so ATP falls. The energy is lost as heat.
Wrong. Falling O2 use fits an electron transport chain inhibitor such as cyanide. A leak makes the chain work harder, not slower.
Wrong. ATP synthesis needs the proton gradient. If protons leak back, there is less drive to make ATP.
Wrong. Glycolysis makes only 2 net ATP and cannot make up the loss. Also, the ETC and gradient are directly affected.

p: The electron transport chain pumps protons out of the matrix to build a gradient. Protons flow back through ATP synthase, which makes ATP. This links (couples) O2 use to ATP making.
An uncoupler lets protons leak back in without passing through ATP synthase. The chain speeds up, O2 use rises, ATP falls, and the extra energy becomes heat.

q17.eli: Picture a water wheel with a hole in the pool above. The pump works nonstop to refill the pool, but the wheel barely turns.
mem: Uncoupler: O2 use up, ATP down, heat up.
Examples: DNP, thermogenin (UCP1) in brown fat.
Inhibitors of the ETC lower O2 use.
q17.trap: Thinking less ATP always means less O2 use. Uncouplers speed up O2 use.

ox: Wrong. CoA attaches to the fatty acid in the cytosol but the acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner membrane by itself.
Correct. Carnitine swaps places with CoA, carries the acyl group across, and CoA is reattached in the matrix, where beta-oxidation occurs.
Wrong. Albumin carries free fatty acids through the blood, not across the mitochondrial membrane.
Wrong. Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the gut through lymph and blood.

p: Beta-oxidation, the breakdown of fatty acids for energy, happens inside the mitochondrial matrix. Long fatty acids must get past the inner mitochondrial membrane, which blocks them.
Carnitine acts as a ferry. It picks up the acyl group, carries it across, and drops it off inside the matrix.

q18.eli: Carnitine is like a ferry that carries cars across a river where no bridge exists.
mem: Carnitine carries long-chain acyl groups into the matrix.
CPT-I is the rate-limiting step; malonyl-CoA inhibits it.
Albumin = blood transport; chylomicron = dietary fat transport.
q18.trap: Picking CoA because it is attached to the fatty acid. It activates it but cannot cross.

ox: Wrong. Liver glycogen runs out within about a day of fasting, so it cannot help by day three.
Correct. Liver turns fatty acids into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate. These cross the blood-brain barrier, so the brain uses them and needs less glucose.
Wrong. Long-chain fatty acids cannot cross the blood-brain barrier well, so the brain does not use them much.
Wrong. Lactate is recycled to glucose through the Cori cycle, which does not reduce the brain's glucose need.

p: During fasting, the body first uses glycogen, then makes glucose from other sources. Over days, the liver breaks down fat and makes ketone bodies, small molecules that can be burned for energy.
The brain can use ketones, so it needs less glucose. This spares muscle protein from being broken down for glucose.

q19.eli: When the gas station is closed, you switch your car to a backup fuel tank.
mem: Ketones: acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate (and acetone).
Made in the liver; used by brain, heart, muscle but not by the liver.
Liver glycogen lasts about 24 hours.
q19.trap: Choosing fatty acids since fat is the source. The brain uses the ketones made from them, not fatty acids directly.
